kjv: moved upon
mine: was hovering over
note: Hebrew merahefet (piel of rahap) describes hovering or fluttering, as a bird over its young (Deut 32:11); "moved" is too vague.

kjv: the first day
mine: one day
note: Hebrew yom ehad uses the cardinal "one," not the ordinal "first" used for later days; the KJV smooths it into a series.

kjv: firmament
mine: vault
note: Hebrew raqia means something hammered out or spread out, a solid dome; "firmament" (Latin firmamentum) keeps the solidity but is now opaque to most readers.

kjv: great whales
mine: great sea creatures
note: Hebrew tanninim are large sea monsters or serpents (elsewhere dragons or serpents), not specifically whales.

kjv: replenish the earth
mine: fill the earth
note: Hebrew mil'u means simply "fill"; in 1611 "replenish" meant fill, but today it suggests refilling a previously populated earth.

kjv: for meat
mine: for food
note: Hebrew le'oklah "for eating"; "meat" meant food in general in 1611, which matters here because the diet given is plants.

kjv: on the seventh day God ended his work
mine: by the seventh day God had finished the work
note: Hebrew wayekal ... bayyom hashevi'i can sound as if God worked on the seventh day; a pluperfect "had finished" (or the LXX/Samaritan "sixth day") avoids the contradiction with "rested."

kjv: a mist
mine: a stream
note: Hebrew 'ed is rare (only here and Job 36:27); comparison with Akkadian edu "flood, underground water" favours a spring or stream rising from the ground.

kjv: a living soul
mine: a living being
note: Hebrew nephesh hayyah is the same phrase used of animals in 1:20-24; "soul" suggests an immortal inner part that the phrase does not specify.

kjv: Ethiopia
mine: Cush
note: Hebrew Kush; the KJV follows the LXX/Vulgate identification with Ethiopia, but the Eden context may point to a region in Mesopotamia (cf. 10:8).

kjv: an help meet for him (the man)
mine: a helper corresponding to him (the man)
note: Hebrew 'ezer kenegdo "a helper fit for / matching him"; KJV "meet" = suitable, which gave rise to the misleading compound "helpmeet."

kjv: Adam
mine: the man
note: Hebrew ha'adam has the article, "the man/human"; the KJV starts using the personal name Adam here, while the Hebrew does so clearly only from 4:25 (or 5:1).

kjv: Ye shall not eat of every tree
mine: You must not eat from any tree
note: Hebrew lo' tokhlu mikkol 'ets means "you shall eat from no tree"; the KJV wording can be read as "not from all (only some) trees," which blunts the serpent's distortion.

kjv: as gods
mine: like God
note: Hebrew ke'lohim can be "like God" or "like gods/divine beings"; since 'elohim in the same verse is God, and 3:22 says "like one of us," either is possible, but the KJV chooses the plural. Context: like God (medium confidence). Elohim earlier in the verse is God, and the serpent promises a share in God's own knowledge; 3:22 'like one of us' confirms divine knowledge, though its plural leaves room for the heavenly council. The plural participle yod'e fits either reading. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and CSB have 'like God'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'like gods' — LXX hos theoi, Vulgate sicut dii, KJV; (2) 'like divine beings', i.e. members of the heavenly council (cf. 3:22 'one of us') — NJPS, NET; (3) 'like great ones/princes' — Targum Onkelos, avoiding a direct comparison with God.

kjv: it (the woman's offspring) shall bruise thy (the serpent's) head
mine: He (the woman's offspring) will strike your (the serpent's) head
note: Hebrew hu' (masculine) refers to zera' "offspring"; the KJV's "it" treats the offspring collectively while "his heel" in the same verse is personal. The verb shuph is better "strike/crush" than "bruise." Traditionally read messianically.

kjv: cursed is the ground for thy (Adam's) sake
mine: cursed is the ground because of you (Adam)
note: Hebrew ba'avurekha means "on account of you"; modern "for thy sake" suggests "for your benefit."

kjv: from the LORD
mine: with the help of Yahweh
note: Hebrew 'et-YHWH is unusual: 'et normally means "with" (or marks an object); "with the help of" is the common reading, while "from" smooths it. Some read "a man, Yahweh," as a messianic claim.

kjv: shalt thou (Cain) not be accepted? ... unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him
mine: will there not be a lifting up? ... its (sin's) desire is for you (Cain), but you must master it
note: Hebrew se'et "lifting up" (of the face, i.e. acceptance or restored countenance); the masculine suffixes in teshuqato and timshol-bo refer to sin pictured as a crouching beast (robets), while KJV "his ... him" is often read as Abel.

kjv: the harp and organ
mine: the lyre and pipe
note: Hebrew kinnor is a lyre and 'ugav a wind instrument (flute or pipe); "organ" now suggests a keyboard instrument.

kjv: an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron
mine: who forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron
note: Hebrew lotesh kol-horesh means "hammering/sharpening every cutting tool"; he is a smith, not a teacher of craftsmen. Nehoshet is copper or bronze, not the zinc alloy brass.

kjv: I (Lamech) have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt
mine: I (Lamech) have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me
note: Hebrew lephits'i ... lehabburati "for my wound ... for my bruise" gives the reason for the killing (revenge for an injury); the KJV phrasing suggests Lamech himself was hurt by killing.

kjv: called their name Adam
mine: named them "Humankind"
note: Hebrew 'adam here names both male and female ("their name"), so it functions as the generic "humankind" rather than the personal name of the first man, though the wordplay with Adam is intended.

kjv: shall not always strive with man
mine: will not remain in humankind forever
note: Hebrew yadon is of uncertain meaning; the ancient versions (LXX katameine, Vulgate permanebit) read "remain/abide," while "strive" derives it from din "judge, contend."

kjv: giants
mine: Nephilim
note: Hebrew nephilim is a transliterated term of unclear meaning (perhaps "fallen ones"); "giants" comes from the LXX gigantes and Num 13:33, and states as fact what the text leaves as a name. Context: keep the name Nephilim; remembered as huge (medium confidence). Nephilim is a term of uncertain meaning, best transliterated, as ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, CSB and NET do. Num 13:33 links them with the gigantic Anakim, so 'giants' reflects how Israel remembered them, but rendering 'giants' turns an interpretation into the word's meaning. Other possible meanings: (1) 'giants' — LXX gigantes, Vulgate, KJV, supported by Num 13:33 and later Jewish tradition (1 Enoch, Jubilees); (2) 'fallen ones' (from naphal) — Genesis Rabbah and some modern scholars, sometimes linked with fallen angels; (3) 'assailants/violent ones' — Aquila (epipiptontes), Symmachus (biaioi); (4) 'mighty men' — Targum Onkelos (gibbaraya).

kjv: it repented the LORD
mine: Yahweh regretted
note: Hebrew wayyinnahem means to regret or be sorry; modern "repent" suggests turning from sin, which misleads when said of God.

kjv: perfect in his (Noah's) generations
mine: blameless among the people of his (Noah's) time
note: Hebrew tamim means whole, sound, blameless; "perfect" in 1611 had this sense but now implies sinlessness.

kjv: A window
mine: a roof
note: Hebrew tsohar occurs only here; it may mean an opening for light (from tsohorayim "noon") or a roof (cf. Akkadian), and "finish it to a cubit above" fits a roof or an eaves-gap.

kjv: by sevens, the male and his female
mine: seven pairs, a male and its mate
note: Hebrew shiv'ah shiv'ah 'ish we'ishto "seven seven, a man and his wife" can mean seven individuals or seven pairs; the pairing language ("a male and its mate") favours seven pairs, while the KJV leaves it open.

kjv: for man's sake
mine: because of humankind
note: Hebrew ba'avur ha'adam means "on account of humankind"; modern "for man's sake" suggests "for man's benefit."

kjv: for the imagination of man's heart is evil
mine: even though the inclination of the human heart is evil
note: Hebrew ki can be causal ("for") or concessive ("although"); since human evil was the reason for the flood (6:5), the concessive reading makes better sense of God's promise not to repeat it.

kjv: replenish the earth
mine: fill the earth
note: Hebrew mil'u "fill"; as in 1:28, modern "replenish" wrongly implies refilling.

kjv: Noah began to be an husbandman, and he planted a vineyard
mine: Noah, a man of the soil, was the first to plant a vineyard
note: Hebrew wayyahel noah 'ish ha'adamah wayyitta' karem: "began" (wayyahel) governs the planting, with "man of the soil" in apposition; Noah was already a farmer (5:29), what is new is viticulture.

kjv: his (Noah's) younger son
mine: his (Noah's) youngest son
note: Hebrew beno haqqatan "his small/young son" is superlative among three sons; Ham is listed second, which has prompted debate, but the Hebrew superlative is the natural sense.

kjv: the isles of the Gentiles
mine: the coastland peoples
note: Hebrew 'iyyey haggoyim "coastlands of the nations"; "Gentiles" (non-Jews) is anachronistic before Israel exists, and 'iyyim covers coasts as well as islands.

kjv: Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh
mine: From that land he (Nimrod) went out to Assyria and built Nineveh
note: Hebrew yatsa' 'ashshur can mean "Asshur went out" (a person) or "he (Nimrod) went out to Assyria" (accusative of direction); Mic 5:6 links Nimrod to Assyria, favouring the latter. Context: Nimrod went to Assyria (medium confidence). 10:8-12 is a single unit on Nimrod's kingdom, Asshur son of Shem appears only at 10:22, and Mic 5:6 calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'; a bare accusative of destination after yatsa' is possible. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, CSB and NET read Nimrod. But every ancient version makes Asshur the subject, so confidence is lowered from high to medium. Other possible meanings: (1) 'Asshur went out (from that land) and built Nineveh', Asshur being a person, ancestor of the Assyrians — LXX, Vulgate, Targum Onkelos, Josephus, KJV, NJPS; (2) the same, with Asshur as the Assyrian people migrating from Babylonia — some commentators.

kjv: the brother of Japheth the elder
mine: the older brother of Japheth
note: Hebrew 'ahi yepheth haggadol is ambiguous: "the elder" may describe Shem or Japheth; the KJV makes Japheth the elder.

kjv: as they journeyed from the east
mine: as people journeyed in the east
note: Hebrew miqqedem can mean "from the east," "eastward," or "in the east" (as in 2:8, where the KJV has "eastward"); the direction of the migration is unclear.

kjv: slime had they for morter
mine: bitumen for mortar
note: Hebrew hemar is bitumen or asphalt (cf. the bitumen pits of 14:10); "slime" now suggests mud or ooze.

kjv: Now the LORD had said
mine: Yahweh said
note: Hebrew wayyomer is a simple narrative past; the KJV pluperfect places the call back in Ur (harmonising with 15:7 and Acts 7:2), which the Hebrew does not mark.

kjv: curse him that curseth thee (Abram)
mine: whoever treats you (Abram) with contempt I will curse
note: Two different verbs: meqallelkha (qillel, "make light of, disdain") and 'a'or ('arar, "curse"); the KJV levels them into one, losing the contrast between human contempt and divine curse.

kjv: the plain of Moreh
mine: the oak of Moreh
note: Hebrew 'elon is a large tree (oak or terebinth), often a sacred landmark; "plain" follows the Targum and Vulgate.

kjv: toward the south
mine: toward the Negev
note: Hebrew hannegbah names the Negev, the dry region in southern Canaan; "south" hides that it is a specific region.

kjv: so I (Pharaoh) might have taken her (Sarai) to me to wife
mine: so that I (Pharaoh) took her (Sarai) as my wife
note: Hebrew wa'eqqah 'otah li le'ishah is a past consecutive: Pharaoh did take her; the KJV's "might have" suggests it was only a possibility.

kjv: into the south
mine: into the Negev
note: Hebrew hannegbah is the Negev region; "went up out of Egypt ... into the south" is confusing since Abram travels north from Egypt into southern Canaan.

kjv: pitched his (Lot's) tent toward Sodom
mine: moved his (Lot's) tent as far as Sodom
note: Hebrew wayye'ehal 'ad-sedom: 'ad means "as far as, up to"; Lot camped right up to Sodom, not merely facing toward it.

kjv: the plain of Mamre
mine: the oaks of Mamre
note: Hebrew 'elone mamre' "the great trees (oaks/terebinths) of Mamre"; "plain" follows the Targum, as in 12:6.

kjv: king of nations
mine: king of Goiim
note: Hebrew goyim "nations" here is most likely a proper name (perhaps a people of Anatolia or Gutium), parallel to the other kingdoms listed.

kjv: slimepits
mine: bitumen pits
note: Hebrew be'erot hemar "pits of bitumen/asphalt," common around the Dead Sea; "slime" no longer conveys this.

kjv: he (Abram) armed his trained servants
mine: he (Abram) mustered his trained men
note: Hebrew wayyareq literally "he emptied out / drew out," i.e. called up or led out his men; "armed" is an interpretive guess from the Vulgate (numeravit) and LXX tradition.

kjv: on the left hand of Damascus
mine: north of Damascus
note: Hebrew missemo'l "on the left" is an orientation term (facing east, the left is north); a modern reader takes "left hand" literally.

kjv: possessor of heaven and earth
mine: Creator of heaven and earth
note: Hebrew qoneh can mean "acquirer/owner" or "creator/maker" (cf. Ugaritic qny, and Deut 32:6); with heaven and earth as object, "Creator" is now widely preferred.

kjv: he (Abram) gave him (Melchizedek) tithes of all
mine: Abram gave him (Melchizedek) a tenth of everything
note: Hebrew wayyitten-lo has no named subject; context and Heb 7:4 indicate Abram paid Melchizedek, which the KJV leaves ambiguous.

kjv: I (Yahweh) am thy (Abram's) shield, and thy exceeding great reward
mine: I (Yahweh) am your (Abram's) shield; your reward will be very great
note: Hebrew sekharkha harbeh me'od can be a second predicate ("[I am] your very great reward") or a separate clause ("your reward [will be] very great"); the Masoretic accents and harbeh (an infinitive "greatly") favour the latter.

kjv: the steward of my (Abram's) house
mine: the heir of my (Abram's) household
note: Hebrew ben-mesheq beti is obscure (mesheq occurs only here, with a pun on Dammeseq); v. 3 makes clear the point is inheritance, but "steward" and "heir" are both guesses.

kjv: a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp
mine: a smoking firepot and a flaming torch
note: Hebrew tannur is a portable clay oven or firepot and lappid a torch; "furnace" and "lamp" suggest the wrong objects.

kjv: a wild man
mine: a wild donkey of a man
note: Hebrew pere' adam: pere' is the wild ass (onager), an image of untamed independence; the KJV drops the animal and leaves only "wild".

kjv: dwell in the presence of all his (Ishmael's) brethren
mine: live in defiance of all his (Ishmael's) brothers
note: 'al-penei kol-'echav can mean "in front of / east of" or "against, in hostility to"; the parallel "his hand against everyone" favours the hostile sense.

kjv: be thou (Abram) perfect
mine: be blameless
note: tamim means whole or blameless (integrity), not flawless perfection.

kjv: I am the Almighty God
mine: I am El Shaddai, God Almighty
note: 'el shaddai is a divine title of uncertain etymology. "Almighty" follows the Greek pantokrator and the Latin omnipotens.

kjv: in the plains of Mamre
mine: by the oaks of Mamre
note: 'elonei means large trees (oaks or terebinths). "Plains" follows the Targum tradition.

kjv: My Lord
mine: My lord
note: The Masoretes pointed 'adonay as the divine title. I read it as Abraham's polite address to an unrecognised visitor ('adoni/'adonay "my lord/sirs"), which the plural verbs in v. 4 support.

kjv: he (Abraham) took butter, and milk
mine: he (Abraham) took curds and milk
note: chem'ah is curdled milk, like yogurt or soft cheese, not churned butter.

kjv: I (Yahweh) will certainly return unto thee (Abraham) according to the time of life
mine: I (Yahweh) will surely return to you (Abraham) about this time next year
note: ka'et chayyah means "at the time when it lives (again)", that is, when the season comes round. The KJV's literal "time of life" is opaque. Same in v. 14.

kjv: For I (Yahweh) know him (Abraham), that he will command his children
mine: For I (Yahweh) have chosen him (Abraham), so that he may command his children
note: yada' here means "chose, acknowledged" (cf. Amos 3:2), and lema'an 'asher is purposive ("in order that"). The KJV turns God's purpose into a prediction about Abraham's character.

kjv: they (the angels) smote the men ... with blindness
mine: they (the angels) struck the men ... with blinding light
note: sanverim (only here and 2 Kgs 6:18) is a sudden dazzling or disorientation, not ordinary blindness. The men can still grope for the door.

kjv: his (Lot's) sons in law, which married his daughters
mine: his (Lot's) sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters
note: loqchei venotav is a participle, "those taking his daughters". Verse 8 says the daughters are unmarried virgins, which favours betrothed men.

kjv: lest thou (Lot) be consumed in the iniquity of the city
mine: or you (Lot) will be swept away in the punishment of the city
note: 'avon covers both guilt and its punishment. In context the threat is the city's coming punishment.

kjv: behold, he is to thee (Sarah) a covering of the eyes ... thus she was reproved
mine: It is your (Sarah's) vindication before all who are with you, and before everyone you are cleared
note: hu' refers to the payment, not to Abraham. kesut 'einayim ("covering of the eyes") is an idiom for compensation that silences reproach. wenokhachat means "you are vindicated/set right", not "reproved".

kjv: mocking
mine: laughing
note: Hebrew metsaheq (piel of tsahaq, the root of "Isaac") means laughing, playing or jesting; the KJV reads it negatively as "mocking" (cf. Gal 4:29), while the text itself only plays on Isaac's name.

kjv: a bottle of water
mine: a skin of water
note: Hebrew hemet is a leather water-skin; "bottle" meant a leather container in 1611 but now suggests glass.

kjv: my (Abimelech's) son, nor with my son's son
mine: my (Abimelech's) offspring, or with my descendants
note: The rare pair nin and neked (a fixed alliterative phrase) means offspring and posterity in general, not specifically son and grandson.

kjv: a grove
mine: a tamarisk tree
note: Hebrew eshel is the tamarisk tree (Arabic athl); the KJV "grove" follows a guess also used for asherah and loses the single tree.

kjv: God did tempt Abraham
mine: God tested Abraham
note: Hebrew nissah means to test or prove; in 1611 "tempt" could mean test, but today it implies enticing to sin, which the text does not say (cf. Jas 1:13). Context: test (high confidence). Nissah means to test or prove (Exod 16:4; Deut 8:2); 22:12 'now I know that you fear God' states the aim, a test of loyalty, not enticement to sin (Jas 1:13). All major modern translations have 'tested' (NJPS 'put Abraham to the test'). Other possible meanings: (1) 'tempted' — KJV, following Vulgate tentavit and LXX epeirazen, which in their day could mean 'test'; in modern English it implies enticing to sin, which the text does not mean; (2) 'proved' — Geneva Bible; same sense as 'tested'.

kjv: God will provide himself a lamb
mine: God will see to the lamb for himself
note: Hebrew yir'eh-lo hasseh is "will see for himself the lamb", i.e. provide it; the KJV word order invites the reading that God provides himself as the lamb, which the Hebrew does not express.

kjv: Jehovah-jireh
mine: Yahweh will see
note: The name YHWH yir'eh means "Yahweh will see (to it)"; the KJV transliterates it with the hybrid form Jehovah, obscuring the wordplay with v.8 and the saying that follows.

kjv: shall all the nations of the earth be blessed
mine: all the nations of the earth shall find blessing
note: The verb is hithpael (hitbarakhu), normally reflexive: nations will invoke Abraham's offspring in blessing; the KJV follows the passive of the LXX (and Gal 3:8), unlike the niphal in 12:3. Rendered "find blessing" to keep both the passive and the reflexive sense open, as at 26:4.

kjv: Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth
mine: Ephron was sitting among the Hittites
note: Hebrew yoshev can mean dwelling or sitting; since Ephron answers on the spot at the city gate, the scene points to his being seated in the assembly, not merely residing there.

kjv: Mesopotamia
mine: Aram-naharaim
note: Hebrew Aram naharayim ("Aram of the two rivers") is the region of upper Mesopotamia around Haran; the KJV uses the Greek name from the LXX.

kjv: for all the goods of his (the servant's) master were in his hand
mine: with all kinds of his (the servant's) master's good things in his hand
note: The clause vekhol-tuv adonav beyado is circumstantial; it most naturally describes the choice gifts he took along, whereas the KJV "for" makes it a reason (his general authority over the estate).

kjv: a golden earring
mine: a gold nose ring
note: Hebrew nezem can be an ear or nose ring, but v.47 places it "on her nose" (al-appah), so a nose ring is meant here.

kjv: the virgin
mine: the young woman
note: Hebrew ha-almah means a young woman of marriageable age; virginity is stated separately with betulah in v.16. The KJV choice parallels its rendering of almah in Isa 7:14.

kjv: upon her (Rebekah's) face
mine: on her (Rebekah's) nose
note: Hebrew al-appah means "on her nose" (af, nose); the KJV "face" obscures that the nezem was a nose ring.

kjv: Hadar
mine: Hadad
note: The Leningrad Codex reads hadad (as also 1 Chr 1:30); the KJV follows printed Hebrew editions that read hadar, a dalet/resh confusion.

kjv: by their (Ishmael's sons') towns, and by their castles
mine: by their (Ishmael's sons') settlements and their encampments
note: Hebrew hatserim are unwalled settlements and tirot are nomadic encampments or stone enclosures; "towns" and "castles" suggest fortified urban life foreign to these tribes.

kjv: he (Ishmael) died in the presence of all his brethren
mine: He (Ishmael) settled down in defiance of all his kinsmen
note: The verb nafal ("fell") here means settled or camped (fulfilling 16:12, where the same phrase al-pene kol-ehav is used); the KJV takes it as "died", which the verb does not mean here.

kjv: why am I (Rebekah) thus?
mine: why am I (Rebekah) alive?
note: The elliptical lamah zeh anokhi ("why this, I?") is obscure; it is often read as despair over living (cf. 27:46), while the KJV keeps it vague.

kjv: a cunning hunter
mine: a skillful hunter
note: Hebrew yodea tsayid, "knowing game"; "cunning" meant skillful in 1611 but now implies craftiness.

kjv: a plain man
mine: a quiet man
note: Hebrew tam means whole, sound or blameless; in context it contrasts the settled, even-tempered Jacob with the wild Esau. "Plain" now suggests homely looks or simplicity.

kjv: venison
mine: game
note: Hebrew tsayid means any hunted game; "venison" in 1611 meant game generally but now means deer meat only. The same applies throughout ch.27.

kjv: in thy (Isaac's) seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed
mine: by your (Isaac's) offspring all the nations of the earth shall find blessing
note: As in 22:18 the verb is hithpael (hitbarakhu), most naturally reflexive ("bless themselves by", i.e. invoke as a model of blessing); the KJV takes it as passive with the LXX. Context: find blessing (keeps passive and reflexive senses open) (low confidence). The hithpael hitbarakhu (as 22:18) is normally reflexive, 'bless themselves' (cf. 48:20), but the parallel promises use the niphal (12:3; 18:18; 28:14), the hithpael can carry middle/passive force, and LXX, Vulgate and the NT (Acts 3:25; Gal 3:8) read 'be blessed'. The evidence is balanced; 'find blessing' keeps both senses. Other possible meanings: (1) 'shall be blessed' (receive blessing through the offspring) — LXX eneulogethesontai, Vulgate benedicentur, Acts 3:25, Gal 3:8, KJV, ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB; (2) 'shall bless themselves by' (invoke the offspring as a model of blessing, cf. 48:20) — NJPS, NET ('pronounce blessings ... using the name'), NRSV ('gain blessing for themselves'), many critical commentators.

kjv: sporting with
mine: caressing
note: Hebrew metsaheq (the Isaac wordplay again) here denotes conjugal fondling that showed she was his wife; "sporting" now suggests merely playing.

kjv: might lightly have lien with thy (Isaac's) wife
mine: might easily have lain with your (Isaac's) wife
note: Hebrew kim'at, "almost, easily"; KJV "lightly" meant easily, but a modern reader may take it as "casually".

kjv: one of his (Abimelech's) friends
mine: his (Abimelech's) adviser
note: Hebrew merea, "companion, friend", appears to be a court title ("the king's friend", cf. 2 Sam 15:37); the KJV "one of his friends" also needlessly adds "one of".

kjv: Who? where is he that hath taken venison
mine: Who then was it that hunted game
note: Hebrew mi-efo hu: efo is the particle "then, now"; the KJV reads it as ayeh/efoh "where", adding a second question.

kjv: thy (Esau's) dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven
mine: away from the fatness of the earth shall your (Esau's) dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven
note: The preposition min in mishmanne ha-arets can be partitive ("of") as in v.28 or separative ("away from"). Esau's lament that no blessing remains (vv.36-38) and the harsh v.40 favour the separative sense; the KJV gives Esau the same blessing as Jacob.

kjv: when thou (Esau) shalt have the dominion
mine: when you (Esau) grow restless
note: The verb tarid (from rud, to roam or be restless) means breaking loose or growing restive; "have the dominion" follows an older derivation from radah (rule) and is not supported.

kjv: took of the stones of that place, and put them for his (Jacob's) pillows
mine: Taking one of the stones of the place, he (Jacob) put it at his head
note: Hebrew meraashotav means "at his head" (place by the head), not "pillows"; the partitive me-avne takes one stone, as v.18 ("the stone") confirms, while the KJV makes it several.

kjv: a ladder
mine: a stairway
note: Hebrew sullam occurs only here; from salal (to heap up), it likely denotes a ramp or stairway like the stepped approach of a temple tower, rather than a rung ladder.

kjv: How dreadful is this place
mine: How awesome is this place
note: Hebrew nora means fearsome, awe-inspiring; "dreadful" once meant that but now means very bad.

kjv: he (Jacob) was her (Rachel's) father's brother
mine: he (Jacob) was her (Rachel's) father's kinsman
note: Hebrew ah means brother or, broadly, relative; Jacob was Laban's nephew, so the literal "brother" misstates the relationship (likewise "my brother" in v.15).

kjv: Leah was tender eyed
mine: Leah's eyes were weak
note: Hebrew rakkot means soft or delicate; it is unclear whether it praises gentle eyes or marks a lack of lustre, but the contrast with Rachel's beauty suggests a shortcoming.

kjv: Leah was hated
mine: Leah was unloved
note: Hebrew senuah ("hated") is the idiom for the less-favoured wife (cf. Deut 21:15), as v.30 "loved Rachel more than Leah" shows; "hated" overstates it for a modern reader (also v.33).

kjv: A troop cometh
mine: Good fortune has come!
note: The qere ba gad means "fortune has come" (gad = luck, also a deity of fortune, Isa 65:11; the ketiv bgd = "with fortune"); the KJV connects Gad with gedud, "troop", as in 49:19.

kjv: now will my (Leah's) husband dwell with me
mine: now my (Leah's) husband will honor me
note: The verb zabal is rare; related to zebul ("lofty abode") and Ugaritic zbl ("prince"), it is now usually taken as "exalt, honor", though "dwell with" (KJV, from zebul as dwelling) remains possible.

kjv: I (Laban) have learned by experience
mine: I (Laban) have learned by divination
note: Hebrew nihashti is from nahash, the technical verb for divination or omen-reading (cf. 44:5, 15); "by experience" removes the reference to Laban's divining.

kjv: green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree
mine: fresh rods of poplar and almond and plane trees
note: Hebrew livneh is the white poplar or storax, luz is the almond (as in the place name Luz), and armon is the oriental plane tree; hazel and chestnut are not native to the region.

kjv: hath he (Jacob) gotten all this glory
mine: he (Jacob) has gained all this wealth
note: Hebrew kavod (literally "weight") here means wealth or substance, as the context of flocks shows; "glory" suggests honour or splendour.

kjv: the rams which leaped upon the cattle
mine: the male goats that mounted the flock
note: Hebrew attudim are he-goats, not rams; the striped, speckled and spotted animals here are the goats of 30:32-35.

kjv: the images
mine: household gods
note: Hebrew teraphim were household gods or ancestral figurines (Laban calls them "my gods", v.30); "images" is vague and hides their religious and possibly inheritance-related role.

kjv: the camel's furniture
mine: the camel's saddle
note: Hebrew kar haggamal is a camel's saddle or litter; "furniture" in 1611 meant harness or trappings.

kjv: his (Jacob's) eleven sons
mine: his (Jacob's) eleven children
note: Hebrew yeladav means children; the eleven include Dinah (Benjamin is not yet born), so "sons" is inexact. KJV 32:22.

kjv: as a prince hast thou (Jacob) power with God and with men
mine: you (Jacob) have striven with God and with men
note: sarita is from sarah "to strive, contend" (cf. Hos 12:4); the KJV derives it from sar "prince", following a traditional etymology. KJV 32:28.

kjv: he (Jacob) halted upon his thigh
mine: limping because of his (Jacob's) hip
note: Halt meant to limp in 1611 (Hebrew tsolea'); today it reads as "stopped". KJV 32:31.

kjv: the sinew which shrank
mine: the sinew of the thigh
note: gid hannasheh is obscure (traditionally the sciatic nerve); the KJV guesses from a root meaning "to shrink/forget". KJV 32:32.

kjv: I (Esau) will go before thee (Jacob)
mine: I (Esau) will go alongside you (Jacob)
note: lenegdekha means "opposite/in front of" or "alongside". In v. 14 Jacob asks Esau to go ahead, which suggests Esau first offered to escort him.

kjv: Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem
mine: Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem
note: shalem can be a place name or the adjective "whole, safe". It fulfils Jacob's vow in 28:21 (beshalom). The KJV invents a town named Shalem.

kjv: he (Shechem) had wrought folly in Israel
mine: he (Shechem) had done an outrage in Israel
note: nevalah means a vile, sacrilegious act, especially sexual (cf. 2 Sam 13:12). "Folly" now sounds like mere foolishness.

kjv: came upon the city boldly
mine: came against the unsuspecting city
note: betach ("in security") can describe the attackers (boldly) or the city (off guard). Since the townsmen were in pain, the city's defencelessness fits better.

kjv: there was but a little way to come to Ephrath
mine: they (Jacob's household) were still some distance from Ephrath
note: kivrat ha'arets is an unknown measure of distance. The KJV's "but a little way" is a guess.

kjv: duke Teman, duke Omar
mine: chief Teman, chief Omar
note: Hebrew 'alluph means a clan chief or tribal head; "duke" (from Latin dux, leader) now suggests European nobility. The same applies throughout vv. 15-43.

kjv: found the mules in the wilderness
mine: found the hot springs in the wilderness
note: The hapax hayyemim is best understood (with the Vulgate aquas calidas) as hot springs; "mules" follows a Jewish tradition, and mule-breeding was forbidden to Israel anyway.

kjv: a coat of [many] colours
mine: a long robe with sleeves
note: Hebrew ketonet passim probably means a robe reaching to the palms and soles (pas = extremity), i.e. a long-sleeved, full-length garment; "many colours" follows the Septuagint's poikilos and is a guess. Also in vv. 23 and 32. Context: a long robe with sleeves (low confidence). Ketonet passim recurs only in 2 Sam 13:18-19, a princess's garment, so it marks status. Pas 'palm/sole' suggests a robe reaching to wrists and ankles, as Aquila, Symmachus and the LXX of 2 Sam 13:18 (karpotos) took it; but the LXX here and a proposed Akkadian parallel point to colour or ornament. The meaning is genuinely uncertain; confidence lowered. Other possible meanings: (1) 'a coat of many colours / multicolored tunic' — LXX chitona poikilon, Vulgate polymitam, KJV, ESV, NASB; (2) 'an ornate/ornamented robe' (embroidered or with appliqué) — NIV, NJPS, cf. Akkadian kitu pisannu; (3) 'a special tunic', leaving the feature unstated — NET; (4) a tunic of fine wool — Rashi.

kjv: spicery and balm and myrrh
mine: gum, balm, and resin
note: Hebrew nekot and lot are aromatic gums (tragacanth and labdanum/ladanum); lot is not myrrh, which is mor in Hebrew.

kjv: go down into the grave unto my (Jacob's) son
mine: go down to my (Jacob's) son in Sheol
note: Hebrew she'olah is Sheol, the underworld abode of the dead; the KJV alternates between "grave", "hell" and "pit", which obscures that it is one consistent term.

kjv: the Midianites sold him (Joseph)
mine: the Medanites sold him (Joseph)
note: The Masoretic text reads hammedanim (Medanites, cf. Medan in Gen 25:2); the KJV follows the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint and Vulgate, which harmonise with "Midianites" in v. 28.

kjv: sat in an open place
mine: sat at the entrance of Enaim
note: Hebrew petah 'enayim is most likely a place name ("the opening of Enaim", cf. Enam in Josh 15:34); the KJV takes it as a common noun phrase ("opening of the eyes", i.e. a conspicuous spot).

kjv: thy (Judah's) signet, and thy bracelets
mine: your (Judah's) seal and its cord
note: Hebrew petil is a cord or string, here the cord on which the cylinder seal hung; "bracelets" is a guess. Also in v. 25.

kjv: the harlot, that [was] openly by the way side
mine: the shrine prostitute who was at Enaim by the road
note: Hirah uses qedeshah ("consecrated woman", a cult prostitute) rather than zonah (v. 15), a more respectable term; the KJV renders both as "harlot". "Openly" again takes ba'enayim as a common noun rather than the place Enaim.

kjv: to mock us
mine: to make sport of us
note: Hebrew letsaheq (from tsahaq, "laugh, play") here carries a sexual overtone of taking liberties (cf. 26:8 Isaac "sporting" with Rebekah); "mock" suggests only verbal ridicule. Also in v. 17.

kjv: the butler of the king of Egypt
mine: the cupbearer of the king of Egypt
note: Hebrew mashqeh is "one who gives drink", the royal cupbearer, a high court office; "butler" now suggests a head household servant. Recurs through chs. 40-41.

kjv: three white baskets
mine: three baskets of white bread
note: Hebrew salle hori: hori denotes white (fine-flour) bread or cakes, so the baskets hold white bread; the KJV takes it as the colour of the baskets themselves (marginal alternative: "full of holes").

kjv: seven ears of corn
mine: seven ears of grain
note: Hebrew shibbolim are ears of grain (wheat or barley); "corn" in 1611 meant any cereal, but modern (especially American) readers hear maize, unknown in the ancient Near East. Recurs with bar/shever ("corn") through chs. 41-47.

kjv: Bow the knee
mine: Abrek!
note: Hebrew 'avrek is an obscure, probably Egyptian or Akkadian, word (perhaps "Attention!" or a title); "Bow the knee" rests on a folk derivation from Hebrew barak "kneel".

kjv: with sorrow to the grave
mine: down to Sheol in sorrow
note: Hebrew she'olah, "to Sheol", the realm of the dead, not simply the burial place; the same phrase recurs in 44:29 and 44:31.

kjv: spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds
mine: gum and resin, pistachio nuts and almonds
note: Hebrew nekot and lot are aromatic gums (tragacanth, labdanum), not myrrh (mor); botnim are specifically pistachio nuts.

kjv: his (Joseph's) bowels did yearn upon his brother
mine: he (Joseph) was deeply moved over his brother
note: Hebrew nikmeru rahamav, "his compassion grew warm"; rahamim (tender feelings, from rehem "womb") was located in the inner organs, and "bowels" now reads as a purely physical statement.

kjv: messes unto them (Joseph's brothers) ... Benjamin's mess
mine: portions were carried to them (Joseph's brothers) ... Benjamin's portion
note: Hebrew mas'ot are portions of food sent from the host's table; "mess" in 1611 meant a served dish, now it means disorder.

kjv: with sorrow to the grave
mine: down to Sheol in misery
note: Hebrew she'olah, "to Sheol", the underworld realm of the dead; the KJV's "grave" narrows it to burial. Same in v. 31.

kjv: neither [be] earing nor harvest
mine: neither plowing nor harvest
note: Hebrew harish is plowing; "earing" (from Old English erian, to plough) is obsolete and now suggests ears of grain.

kjv: to preserve you (Joseph's brothers) a posterity in the earth
mine: to preserve for you (Joseph's brothers) a remnant on the earth
note: Hebrew she'erit means a remnant or surviving group; "posterity" shifts the sense from survivors now to descendants later.

kjv: corn and bread and meat
mine: grain, bread, and provisions
note: Hebrew mazon is food or provisions in general; "meat" in 1611 meant food, but now suggests flesh.

kjv: Job
mine: Iob
note: Hebrew Yov (called Jashub in Num 26:24 and 1 Chr 7:1) is unrelated to Iyyov, the Job of the book of Job; the KJV spelling suggests the same person.

kjv: with bread, according to [their] families
mine: with food, according to the number of their dependents
note: Hebrew lefi hattaf means "according to the (number of) little ones/dependents", i.e. rations proportioned to household size; "families" loses the reference to the taf.

kjv: guiding his (Israel's) hands wittingly
mine: crossing his (Israel's) hands
note: Hebrew sikkel 'et-yadav: the KJV derives it from sakal "act wisely" (deliberately); most now take it from a homonym "cross, interlace" (so the Targum and Syriac). Either way Jacob's act is intentional.

kjv: one portion above thy (Joseph's) brethren
mine: one mountain slope, over and above your (Joseph's) brothers
note: Hebrew shekhem 'ahad is literally "one shoulder", i.e. a ridge or slope of land, with a pun on the town Shechem (cf. John 4:5); "portion" captures the sense but loses the wordplay and the geography.

kjv: instruments of cruelty are in their (Simeon and Levi's) habitations
mine: their (Simeon and Levi's) blades are weapons of violence
note: mekheroteihem is a hapax, probably "swords/blades" (cf. Greek machaira); the KJV guesses "habitations" from a root meaning "dwell". Context: swords (medium confidence). Mekheroteihem is a hapax. 'Swords/blades' (perhaps related to Greek machaira, as Rashi already noted) fits the recollection of Gen 34:25, where Simeon and Levi 'took their swords', and is the reading of ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, CSB and NET. The derivation remains uncertain. Other possible meanings: (1) 'their habitations / land of sojourning' (from gur) — Targum Onkelos, KJV; (2) 'their origin/kinship' (cf. mekhorah, Ezek 16:3) — some medieval and modern interpreters; (3) 'their schemes' (from karah 'plot') — LXX ex haireseos auton ('of their own choice'), some commentators; (4) 'their weapons' generally — NJPS.

kjv: they (Simeon and Levi) digged down a wall
mine: they (Simeon and Levi) hamstrung oxen
note: 'iqqeru-shor: 'iqqer means to hamstring and shor is "ox"; the KJV read shur "wall" and gave the verb a sense of digging.

kjv: O my (Jacob's) soul, come not thou into their (Simeon and Levi's) secret
mine: Let me (Jacob) not enter their (Simeon and Levi's) council
note: nafshi is idiomatic for "I/myself" and sod means council; the KJV renders both woodenly.

kjv: as an old lion
mine: like a lioness
note: lavi' most likely means lion or lioness, not specifically an old lion.

kjv: until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be
mine: until the One to Whom it belongs comes, and the obedience of the peoples is His
note: shiloh is one of the most debated cruxes: it may be a name, "Shiloh" the town, or shello "(he) to whom it belongs" (cf. Ezek 21:32). yiqqehat means "obedience", not "gathering". Both readings are read messianically. Context: until the One to Whom it belongs comes (medium confidence). Reading shello 'whose it is' has the widest ancient support: Ezek 21:32 (Eng 21:27) 'until he comes whose right it is', LXX (ta apokeimena auto / ho apokeitai), Symmachus, Peshitta and the Targums ('until Messiah comes, whose is the kingdom'). The parallel 'the obedience of the peoples is his' needs a person. NIV and NET agree. Other possible meanings: (1) 'until Shiloh comes', a personal (messianic) name — KJV, NASB, Talmud (Sanh 98b), Genesis Rabbah; (2) 'until tribute comes to him' (shay lo) — ESV, NRSV, NJPS; (3) 'until he comes to Shiloh' (the town) — some medieval and critical scholars; (4) 'until his ruler comes' (Akkadian shelu) — a few modern scholars. Also 'gathering' (KJV) for yiqqehat 'obedience'.

kjv: a lawgiver from between his (Judah's) feet
mine: the ruler's staff from between his (Judah's) feet
note: mechoqeq can mean "commander" or "commander's staff"; the parallel with "scepter" favours the staff.

kjv: His (Judah's) eyes shall be red with wine
mine: His (Judah's) eyes are darker than wine
note: chakhlili is rare ("dull/dark" or "sparkling"); the min can be comparative ("than wine") or causal ("from wine").

kjv: couching down between two burdens
mine: lying down between the sheepfolds
note: mishpetayim (dual) most likely means sheepfolds or saddlebags; "two burdens" is a guess.

kjv: a troop shall overcome him (Gad): but he shall overcome at the last
mine: raiders shall raid him (Gad), but he shall raid at their heels
note: The verse puns on gad/gedud/yagud; 'aqev means "heel", not "at the last".

kjv: whose branches run over the wall
mine: its shoots climb over the wall
note: banot tsa'adah, literally "daughters (that) step", is obscure. Some read it as wild asses ("Joseph is a wild colt"), not a vine.

kjv: Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf
mine: Benjamin is a ravenous wolf
note: Ravin (to devour, plunder) is obsolete; the Hebrew ze'ev yitraf means "a wolf that tears".

kjv: were brought up upon Joseph's knees
mine: were born on Joseph's knees
note: yulledu 'al-birkei means "were born upon the knees", an adoption or legitimation rite (cf. 30:3), not upbringing.

kjv: God will surely visit you (Joseph's brothers)
mine: God will surely take note of you (Joseph's brothers)
note: paqod yifqod means God will attend to them and intervene to rescue them. "Visit" now suggests a social call. Same in v. 25.

kjv: treasure cities
mine: storage cities
note: 'arei miskenot are supply depots for grain and stores, not treasuries.

kjv: they (the Egyptians) were grieved because of the children of Israel
mine: the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites
note: wayyaqutsu means they felt loathing or dread (cf. Num 22:3), not sorrow.

kjv: he (God) made them (the midwives) houses
mine: he (God) gave them (the midwives) households of their own
note: 'asah lahem battim means God gave the midwives families or descendants. It is not literal house-building.

kjv: an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime
mine: a basket made of papyrus reeds, coated it with tar
note: teivat gome' is a papyrus basket; tevah is also Noah's "ark". chemar is bitumen, not "slime".

kjv: the backside of the desert
mine: the far side of the wilderness
note: Hebrew 'ahar hammidbar means behind/beyond (i.e. west of) the wilderness; "backside" now reads oddly and the area is steppe pasture rather than desert.

kjv: I (Yahweh) have surely visited you (Israel)
mine: I (Yahweh) have surely taken note of you (Israel)
note: paqad paqadti means to attend to or take action on someone's behalf; modern "visited" suggests a social call.

kjv: every woman shall borrow of her neighbour
mine: Each woman shall ask of her neighbor
note: sha'al means to ask or request; nothing implies a loan to be returned, and the outcome is that Israel "plunders" (natsal) Egypt.

kjv: jewels of silver, and jewels of gold
mine: articles of silver and articles of gold
note: kele kesef = vessels/objects of silver (any manufactured item), not specifically gems or jewellery as "jewels" now implies.

kjv: leprous as snow
mine: diseased, white as snow
note: metsora'at denotes the skin affliction tsara'at, a range of flaking skin conditions, not Hansen's disease as "leprous" now suggests.

kjv: Jethro his (Moses') father in law
mine: his (Moses') father-in-law Jether
note: The Hebrew has the short form Yeter here (Yitro later in the verse); the KJV silently normalises to Jethro.

kjv: and if thou (Pharaoh) refuse to let him (Israel) go, behold, I (Yahweh) will slay
mine: but you (Pharaoh) refused to let him (Israel) go. Now I (Yahweh) am going to kill
note: wattema'en is a past narrative form ("and you refused"), stating Pharaoh's refusal as fact, not a condition.

kjv: by the way in the inn
mine: at a lodging place on the way
note: malon is a night camp or stopping place; "inn" suggests a building with a host.

kjv: cast it at his feet
mine: touched his feet with it
note: wattagga' (hiphil of naga') means "made it touch"; she applied the foreskin to his feet (whose feet is ambiguous), not threw it.

kjv: a bloody husband
mine: a bridegroom of blood
note: hatan damim is "bridegroom/son-in-law of blood", a ritual phrase tied to circumcision; "bloody husband" now sounds like a curse or a violent husband.

kjv: the words of the LORD who had sent him (Moses)
mine: the words of Yahweh with which He had sent him (Moses)
note: 'asher shelaho refers to the words he was sent with, not to Yahweh as the sender.

kjv: let the people from their works
mine: taking the people away from their work
note: tapri'u (para') means to draw away or release from work; KJV "let ... from" uses "let" in its old sense of keep/hinder, which a modern reader cannot parse.

kjv: the tale of the bricks
mine: the same quota of bricks
note: matkonet means the fixed amount or quota; "tale" is old English for a count (also 5:18, tokhen).

kjv: by my name JEHOVAH
mine: by My name Yahweh
note: YHWH is spelled out here as "JEHOVAH", a hybrid of the consonants YHWH with the vowels of Adonai; elsewhere the KJV writes LORD. The name was most likely pronounced Yahweh. Context: known in the character the name expresses (medium confidence). Genesis uses the name Yahweh, even in God's speech to the patriarchs (15:7; 28:13). In 6:6-7 'you shall know that I am Yahweh' means experiencing the name through redemption, so the contrast is one of revelation, not vocabulary. The rendering keeps the Hebrew open; the KJV difference is only the form of the name. Other possible meanings: (1) the name itself was unknown before Moses, and Genesis uses it anachronistically — many source-critical scholars (assigning 6:3 to P); (2) a rhetorical question, 'by my name Yahweh did I not make myself known to them?' — a minority of interpreters; (3) the patriarchs received the promises but not their fulfilment, which the name signifies — Rashi.

kjv: mine armies, [and] my people
mine: My divisions, My people the Israelites
note: tsiv'otai ("my hosts/divisions") stands in apposition to "my people"; the KJV's supplied "and" makes them sound like two different groups.

kjv: And he (Yahweh) hardened Pharaoh's heart
mine: Yet Pharaoh's heart was hardened
note: wayyehezaq lev par'oh is an intransitive qal ("Pharaoh's heart grew hard"); the KJV makes God the active subject here, though the text leaves the agent unstated (cf. 7:22, same verb, which the KJV renders passively).

kjv: the Egyptians shall lothe to drink
mine: the Egyptians will be unable to drink
note: nil'u (la'ah) means to be weary or to strive in vain; the point is that they will be unable to drink it (cf. 7:21), not that they will feel disgust.

kjv: lice
mine: gnats
note: kinnim/kinnam is an uncertain insect name; ancient versions (LXX skniphes) and modern lexica favour gnats or mosquitoes rather than lice (KJV 8:16-18).

kjv: swarms [of flies]
mine: swarms
note: 'arov means "swarm/mixture"; the KJV supplies "of flies" (after the LXX "dog-fly"), but the creature is not specified (KJV 8:21-31).

kjv: the LORD in the midst of the earth
mine: Yahweh in the midst of the land
note: ha'arets here most naturally means the land of Egypt, where Yahweh shows he is active, not the whole earth (KJV 8:22).

kjv: I (Yahweh) will put a division
mine: I (Yahweh) will put redemption
note: The Masoretic text reads pedut "redemption/ransom"; the KJV "division" follows the LXX/Vulgate sense (perhaps reading pelut "separation") (KJV 8:23).

kjv: For now I (Yahweh) will stretch out my hand, that I may smite thee (Pharaoh)
mine: For by now I (Yahweh) could have stretched out My hand and struck you (Pharaoh)
note: shalahti is perfect with 'attah ("by now"), used counterfactually: God could already have wiped Pharaoh out (and v.16 explains why he has not). The KJV turns it into a future threat that is never carried out.

kjv: for this [cause] have I (Yahweh) raised thee (Pharaoh) up
mine: for this reason I (Yahweh) have let you (Pharaoh) remain
note: he'emadtika (hiphil of 'amad) means "I have caused you to stand / kept you standing", i.e. let you survive; "raised thee up" (cf. Rom 9:17, exegeira) can suggest bringing Pharaoh to power.

kjv: mighty thunderings
mine: God's thunder
note: qolot 'elohim is literally "voices/thunders of God"; the KJV takes 'elohim as a superlative ("mighty"), a possible idiom, but the plain sense ties the thunder to God.

kjv: the wheat and the rie
mine: the wheat and the spelt
note: kussemet is spelt or emmer wheat, a grain grown in Egypt; rye was not cultivated there.

kjv: what things I (Yahweh) have wrought in Egypt
mine: how I (Yahweh) dealt harshly with the Egyptians
note: hit'allalti (hithpael of 'alal) means to deal ruthlessly with or make sport of someone; the KJV's neutral "wrought" loses the note of humiliating Egypt.

kjv: into thy (Pharaoh's) coast
mine: into your (Pharaoh's) territory
note: gevul means border or territory; "coast" in 1611 meant a border region, but now suggests the seashore (also 10:14, 10:19).

kjv: let every man borrow of his neighbour
mine: that every man ask of his neighbor
note: As in 3:22, yish'alu (sha'al) means to ask or request; "borrow" implies a promise to return the goods, which the text does not contain.

kjv: shall kill it (the lamb) in the evening
mine: shall slaughter it (the lamb) at twilight
note: ben ha'arbayim is literally "between the two evenings", usually understood as the time between sunset and dark (or late afternoon to sunset); "in the evening" smooths over a phrase whose exact limits were later debated.

kjv: nor sodden at all with water
mine: or boiled in water
note: bashel mevushshal means boiled/cooked; "sodden" (old past participle of seethe) now means soaked.

kjv: they (the Israelites) borrowed of the Egyptians
mine: had asked the Egyptians for
note: wayyish'alu (sha'al) means they asked or requested; there is no loan, and v.36 calls the result plunder.

kjv: so that they (the Egyptians) lent unto them (the Israelites)
mine: so that they (the Egyptians) granted what they (the Israelites) asked
note: wayyash'ilum (hiphil of sha'al) means "they let them have what they asked"; "lent" implies return, contradicting "they plundered (natsal) the Egyptians".

kjv: when Pharaoh would hardly let us go
mine: when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go
note: hiqshah par'oh leshallehenu means Pharaoh "made it hard" (was obstinate) about releasing them; modern "hardly" (= barely) almost reverses the sense.

kjv: Lest peradventure the people repent
mine: The people might change their minds
note: yinnahem (niphal of naham) here means to change one's mind or regret, not moral repentance.

kjv: went up harnessed
mine: went up ... equipped for battle
note: hamushim is rare; probably "armed / in battle formation" (some connect it with "five", i.e. in ranks). "Harnessed" (= in armour) is now opaque.

kjv: He (Yahweh) took not away the pillar
mine: The pillar ... did not depart
note: lo yamish is intransitive ("did not move away"), with the pillar as subject; the KJV makes God the subject.

kjv: it (the pillar of cloud) was a cloud and darkness [to them], but it gave light by night [to these:]
mine: There was the cloud and the darkness, yet it (the pillar of cloud) lit up the night
note: The Hebrew is terse and obscure (wayehi he'anan wehahoshekh wayya'er et-hallaylah); the KJV's supplied words resolve it as darkness for Egypt and light for Israel, a plausible but added interpretation.

kjv: took off their (the Egyptians') chariot wheels
mine: He (Yahweh) jammed the wheels of their (the Egyptians') chariots
note: MT wayyasar means "he removed / turned aside"; the LXX and Samaritan read wayye'sor "he bound (clogged)". The following "drove with difficulty" suits clogged rather than missing wheels.

kjv: the sea returned to his strength
mine: the sea returned to its normal flow
note: le'etano is from 'etan "perennial, constant"; it means the sea's usual state or full flow, not its "strength".

kjv: I will prepare him (God) an habitation
mine: I will praise Him (God)
note: 'anvehu is probably "I will praise/adorn him" (cf. naveh "beautiful"); the KJV derived it from naveh "abode". Context: I will praise Him (medium confidence). The parallel 'I will exalt him' and the LXX (doxaso) and Vulgate (glorificabo) favour 'praise/glorify' (from naweh 'be beautiful, fitting'), as nearly all major translations render. But naveh 'abode' recurs in the same song (15:13, 17), so the Targum's 'build him a sanctuary' is a real possibility; confidence lowered from high to medium. Other possible meanings: (1) 'I will prepare him a habitation / enshrine him' (from naveh 'abode') — Targum Onkelos, KJV, NJPS ('enshrine Him'); (2) 'I will adorn him', honouring him with beautiful worship — Mekhilta, Rashi; (3) 'I will be like him' (ani wahu) — Abba Shaul in Mekhilta and Talmud (Shab 133b).

kjv: the inhabitants of Palestina
mine: the inhabitants of Philistia
note: Hebrew peleshet is the coastal land of the Philistines; "Palestina" suggests the much larger later Roman province.

kjv: the dukes of Edom
mine: the chiefs of Edom
note: 'allufei are clan chiefs; "dukes" imports European nobility.

kjv: The people shall hear, and be afraid
mine: The peoples have heard; they tremble
note: The Hebrew perfects (shame'u) can be prophetic future or past; the KJV makes vv. 14-16 future, and mine reads them as accomplished.

kjv: a small round thing
mine: a fine, flaky substance
note: mechuspas is a hapax, probably "flaky" or "scale-like". "Round" is a guess from the Vulgate.

kjv: they (the Israelites) said one to another, It is manna: for they wist not what it was
mine: they (the Israelites) said to one another, "What is it?"—for they did not know what it was
note: man hu' is a question, "What is it?" (man = "what"). The name "manna" (v. 31) comes from this pun. The KJV makes them name it because they did not know what it was, which does not hold together.

kjv: wherefore do ye (the people) tempt the LORD?
mine: Why do you (the people) test Yahweh?
note: nissah means to test or put to the proof. Today "tempt" means to entice to sin. Same in v. 7.

kjv: Joshua discomfited Amalek
mine: Joshua overwhelmed Amalek
note: wayyachalosh means he defeated or disabled them. "Discomfited" now means made uneasy.

kjv: Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war
mine: A hand upon the throne of Yah!
note: yad 'al-kes yah is obscure: "kes" is not a known word; it is read as a short form of kisse' "throne" (the KJV, following the Targum, takes "hand upon the throne" as an oath) or as nes "banner". Context decides for "banner": v.15 names the altar Yahweh-nissi, "Yahweh is my banner", and Moses' raised hands (17:11-12) are the rallying sign of the battle. Context: A hand upon the throne of Yah (medium confidence). MT kes is most simply a short form of kisse' 'throne'; the Samaritan Pentateuch reads ks', and the Vulgate (solii) and Targums read 'throne'. 'Banner' requires emending kes to nes, attractive after v.15 (Yahweh-nissi) but unsupported by any witness. ESV, NIV, NJPS, CSB and NET read 'throne'. Whose hand, raised in oath or against the throne, is left open. Other possible meanings: (1) 'a hand upon the banner of Yah' (emending to nes, cf. 17:15) — NRSV, many critical commentators; (2) an oath, 'Yahweh has sworn' (hand raised upon the throne) — Targum, Rashi, KJV, NASB95; (3) Amalek's hand raised against Yahweh's throne — NIV; (4) 'with a hidden hand' (from ksh 'cover') — LXX.

kjv: for in the thing wherein they (the Egyptians) dealt proudly he (Yahweh) was above them (the Egyptians)
mine: because of what happened when they (the Egyptians) acted arrogantly against the people
note: The Hebrew ki baddavar 'asher zadu 'aleihem is elliptical, with no main verb. The KJV adds "he was above them". I take it as referring to Egypt's arrogance and what befell them.

kjv: a peculiar treasure unto me
mine: My treasured possession
note: segullah means a personal treasure or private property. "Peculiar" meant "one's own" in 1611 but now means "odd".

kjv: There shall not an hand touch it
mine: No hand shall touch him (whoever touches the mountain)
note: bo can mean "it" (the mountain) or "him" (the trespasser). Since the offender is to be stoned or shot from a distance, it most likely means "him".

kjv: God answered him (Moses) by a voice
mine: God would answer him (Moses) in thunder
note: beqol can mean "with a voice" or "in thunder". qolot means thunder in v. 16.

kjv: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain
mine: You shall not take up the name of Yahweh your God for falsehood
note: lo' tissa' ... lashshaw' means "lift up (the name) for emptiness/falsehood". It probably refers mainly to false oaths, not just casual speech. "In vain" narrows it to profanity.

kjv: Thou shalt not kill
mine: You shall not murder
note: ratsach means unlawful killing (murder, manslaughter). The law prescribes the death penalty and war in the same corpus, so "kill" is too broad.

kjv: in all places where I record my name
mine: In every place where I cause My name to be remembered
note: 'azkir (hiphil of zakar) means "cause to be remembered/invoked". "Record" now suggests writing down.

kjv: his master shall bring him unto the judges
mine: his master shall bring him to God
note: ha'elohim is "God" (perhaps at the sanctuary, or household gods at the doorpost). The KJV follows the Targum in reading it as "judges". Same issue in 22:7-8. Context: to God (medium confidence). Ha'elohim is normally 'God'; 22:7-8 uses the same phrase for a verdict, there with a plural verb, which some take as 'judges'. The rite at the door may be at the sanctuary or the household doorpost. ESV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS read 'God'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'to the judges' — Targum Onkelos, Rashi, KJV, NIV, CSB, NET, taking elohim as judges acting for God (cf. Ps 82:6); (2) 'to the tribunal of God' — LXX pros to kriterion tou theou; (3) 'to the (household) gods' at the doorpost — Vulgate diis, some scholars on ancient Near Eastern analogies.

kjv: he (the master) shall be surely punished
mine: he (the slave) shall surely be avenged
note: naqom yinnaqem means "he (the slave) shall be avenged", implying blood vengeance or the death penalty. "Punished" leaves the penalty vague.

kjv: so that her fruit depart from her, and yet no mischief follow
mine: so that her children come out, but there is no serious harm
note: weyatse'u yeladeiha ("her children come out") may mean premature live birth or miscarriage, and the 'ason ("serious harm") of vv. 22-23 may refer to the mother, the child, or both. The passage is much debated, and both renderings keep it ambiguous. Context: open; a premature live birth is slightly favoured (low confidence). Yatsa' is used of live birth (Gen 25:25-26) and yeladim of living children, and 'no harm' follows the birth; but whether the 'ason of vv. 22-23 refers to the mother, the child or both is not stated. The literal rendering keeps the question open, as the KJV's 'her fruit depart' also does. Other possible meanings: (1) 'she miscarries', with the harm of v. 23 concerning the mother — LXX (penalty depending on whether the foetus was formed), Philo, Mekhilta, NRSV, NJPS; (2) 'she gives birth prematurely', so that v. 23 covers harm to mother or child — NIV, NASB, CSB, NET.

kjv: brought unto the judges
mine: come near to God
note: Hebrew ha-elohim, normally "God"; KJV (with Targum tradition) takes it as human judges, but the case is brought to God, likely at the sanctuary by oath or oracle (KJV 22:8).

kjv: before the judges; whom the judges shall condemn
mine: before God; the one whom God declares guilty
note: Again ha-elohim / elohim (with plural verb yarshi'un); best read as God giving a verdict at the sanctuary rather than a panel of judges (KJV 22:9).

kjv: the dowry of virgins
mine: the bride-price for virgins
note: mohar is the price paid by the groom to the bride's father, not a dowry brought by the bride (KJV 22:17).

kjv: a witch
mine: a sorceress
note: mekhashefah is a female practitioner of sorcery or magic; "witch" carries later European associations that shaped how the verse was used (KJV 22:18).

kjv: usurer; usury
mine: creditor; interest
note: neshekh is any interest on a loan, not only excessive interest as "usury" now means (KJV 22:25).

kjv: revile the gods
mine: revile God
note: elohim here is most naturally "God" (paired with the human chief, nasi); KJV's "the gods" (or judges) follows a traditional reading (KJV 22:28). Context: God (medium confidence). Elohim with a singular sense is normal, and the pairing with the human chief (nasi) sets divine and human authority side by side. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, CSB and NET read 'God'. Acts 23:5 quotes only the second line. Other possible meanings: (1) 'the gods' (do not revile other peoples' gods) — LXX theous, Vulgate diis, Philo, Josephus, KJV; (2) 'the judges' — Targum Onkelos (dayyana), Mekhilta, Rashi, cf. 21:6.

kjv: take no gift: for the gift blindeth
mine: not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds
note: shochad is specifically a bribe or payment to influence a judgment; "gift" now suggests any present.

kjv: their images
mine: their standing stones
note: matsevot are upright stone pillars (massebot) used in Canaanite cult, not carved images.

kjv: will destroy all the people
mine: will throw into confusion all the people
note: hammoti from hamam means to throw into panic or rout, a holy-war terror motif, rather than to destroy outright.

kjv: a sapphire stone
mine: lapis lazuli
note: sappir in antiquity denoted the deep-blue lapis lazuli, which fits "like the very heavens"; the modern sapphire (corundum) was little known then.

kjv: badgers' skins
mine: fine leather
note: tachash is uncertain (perhaps dugong/sea-cow hide or a fine treated leather, cf. Egyptian ths); badgers are not native to the region and the KJV guess is now generally rejected.

kjv: in the four corners thereof (the ark)
mine: on its (the ark's) four feet
note: pa'amot means feet (or bases), not corners.

kjv: a mercy seat
mine: an atonement cover
note: kapporet derives from kipper "atone/cover"; it is the lid of the ark, the place of atonement. "Mercy seat" (Tyndale, after Luther's Gnadenstuhl) is interpretive rather than a rendering of the word.

kjv: bowls thereof, to cover withal
mine: bowls with which to pour drink offerings
note: yussakh bahen is from nasakh "pour out (a libation)"; KJV derived it from sakhakh "cover".

kjv: a candlestick
mine: a lampstand
note: menorah held seven oil lamps (25:37), not candles.

kjv: his (the lampstand's) shaft, and his branches
mine: its (the lampstand's) base and its shaft
note: yerekh is the base (lit. thigh) and qaneh here is the central shaft; the six branches are listed separately in 25:32.

kjv: badgers' skins
mine: fine leather
note: tachash is uncertain (dugong/sea-cow hide or specially treated leather); "badgers" is an outdated guess.

kjv: boards
mine: upright frames
note: qerashim (10 x 1.5 cubits, with two tenons) are now usually understood as open frames rather than solid planks, which would have been impossibly heavy.

kjv: the tabernacle of the congregation
mine: the tent of meeting
note: ohel mo'ed is the tent where God meets (ya'ad, cf. 25:22; 29:42-43) with Moses and Israel; KJV's rendering suggests a place where the congregation assembles. Recurs throughout chs. 27-31 and 33-35.

kjv: wise hearted... the spirit of wisdom
mine: the skilled... a spirit of skill
note: chakhme-lev / ruach chokhmah here denote technical craftsmanship (tailoring), not wisdom in the moral or intellectual sense.

kjv: a mitre, and a girdle
mine: a turban, and a sash
note: mitsnefet is a wound linen turban and avnet a waist sash; "mitre" now suggests a bishop's peaked hat and "girdle" a corset.

kjv: the curious girdle
mine: the skillfully woven band
note: chesheb is a woven waistband; "curious" in 1611 meant skillfully wrought.

kjv: at the ends
mine: twisted like cords
note: migbalot (cf. gavlut 28:22) means twisted/braided, not "at the borders/ends" as KJV derived it from gevul.

kjv: a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle
mine: carnelian, chrysolite, and emerald
note: The identification of the breastpiece gems (odem, pitdah, bareqet) is uncertain; modern mineralogy and ancient usage suggest different stones from KJV's (largely LXX/Vulgate-based) list.

kjv: an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond
mine: a turquoise, a lapis lazuli, and a moonstone
note: nofekh, sappir, yahalom: sappir is lapis lazuli; yahalom cannot be diamond, which ancient craftsmen could not engrave (28:21); its identity is uncertain.

kjv: a ligure
mine: a jacinth
note: leshem is an unidentified stone (LXX ligurion); "ligure" is an obsolete name.

kjv: the caul that is above the liver
mine: the lobe of the liver
note: yoteret is the appendage (caudate lobe) of the liver, not the caul (omentum).

kjv: an offering made by fire
mine: a food offering
note: ishsheh was traditionally linked to esh "fire"; many now connect it with a word for gift/food (Ugaritic itt), since it is used even of offerings not burned.

kjv: the rump... the right shoulder
mine: the fat tail... the right thigh
note: alyah is the fat tail of the sheep; shoq is the leg/thigh, not the shoulder (also 29:27).

kjv: the meat offering
mine: a grain offering
note: minchah here is the flour-and-oil offering of 29:40; "meat" in 1611 meant food in general, but modern readers take it as animal flesh.

kjv: a stranger shall not eat
mine: an outsider shall not eat
note: zar here means anyone not of the priestly family (a layperson), not a foreigner as "stranger" suggests.

kjv: a ransom for his soul
mine: a ransom for his life
note: nefesh here is the person's life (spared from plague), not the "soul" in a later spiritual sense; likewise "atonement for your souls" in 30:15-16.

kjv: upon a stranger
mine: on an outsider
note: zar is a non-priest (layperson), not a foreigner.

kjv: tempered together
mine: seasoned with salt
note: memullach is "salted" (from melach "salt"; cf. Lev 2:13); KJV took it as "mixed".

kjv: the cloths of service
mine: the finely woven garments
note: bigde ha-serad is obscure; serad likely denotes plaited or finely woven work, and the phrase refers to garments (the priestly vestments), not service cloths for wrapping furniture as KJV took it.

kjv: rose up to play
mine: rose up to revel
note: letsacheq (piel of tsachaq) suggests festive, possibly licentious revelry and dancing (cf. 32:19), stronger than modern "play".

kjv: repent of this evil against thy (Yahweh's) people
mine: relent from this disaster against Your (Yahweh's) people
note: hinnachem means to relent or change course and ra'ah here is harm/disaster, not moral evil; "repent of evil" now implies God had done wrong.

kjv: the LORD repented of the evil which he thought to do
mine: Yahweh relented from the disaster that He had said He would do
note: vayyinnachem = relented; ra'ah = calamity; and dibber is "spoke/said", not "thought".

kjv: the people were naked... Aaron had made them naked
mine: the people had broken loose... Aaron had let them break loose
note: para' means to let loose, let run wild (cf. Prov 29:18), not to strip; KJV followed a traditional sense "uncover".

kjv: For Moses had said, Consecrate yourselves (the sons of Levi)
mine: And Moses said, "Ordain yourselves (the sons of Levi)
note: MT has a simple narrative vayyomer after the slaughter, commending the Levites ("fill your hand" = ordination idiom); KJV's pluperfect moves the command before the killing.

kjv: in the day when I (Yahweh) visit I will visit their (the people's) sin upon them
mine: on the day when I (Yahweh) punish, I will punish them (the people) for their sin
note: paqad here means to call to account, punish; "visit" no longer carries this sense for most readers.

kjv: I (Yahweh) will come up into the midst of thee (Israel) in a moment, and consume thee
mine: if for a single moment I (Yahweh) should go up among you (Israel), I would consume you
note: The clause rega' echad e'eleh beqirbekha wekhillitikha is hypothetical, explaining why God will not go among them (33:3); KJV reads it as an actual threat.

kjv: by the mount Horeb
mine: from Mount Horeb onward
note: mehar Chorev "from Mount Horeb" most naturally means from that point on; KJV makes it a location.

kjv: Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it
mine: Moses used to take the tent and pitch it
note: The verbs in 33:7-11 are frequentative (yiqqach... venatah), describing a regular practice; and ha-ohel is a simple tent, not the tabernacle (mishkan) still to be built.

kjv: visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children
mine: bringing the iniquity of the fathers on the children
note: poqed avon means to bring the consequences of iniquity to account; "visit" in this punitive sense is now obscure.

kjv: break their images, and cut down their groves
mine: smash their standing stones and cut down their Asherah poles
note: matsevot are cultic stone pillars and asherim are wooden cult objects (poles or stylised trees) associated with the goddess Asherah, not groves of trees.

kjv: in earing time
mine: in plowing time
note: charish is plowing; "earing" (from Old English erian, to plow) is now misread as the time of ears of grain.

kjv: while he (Moses) talked with him (Yahweh)
mine: because he (Moses) had been talking with Him (Yahweh)
note: bedabbero ito can be temporal or causal; the shining resulted from Moses' speaking with God, and he was no longer talking at the moment of descent.

kjv: till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face
mine: When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face
note: vaykhal Moshe middabber means "Moses finished speaking"; he veiled himself after delivering God's words (34:34-35), not while speaking as the KJV's supplied "till" implies. Relevant to Paul's use in 2 Cor 3:13.

kjv: badgers' skins
mine: fine leather
note: tachash is uncertain: possibly dugong or dolphin skin, or fine dyed leather (cf. Egyptian ths). Badgers are unlikely. Same in v. 23 and 36:19.

kjv: the mercy seat
mine: the atonement cover
note: kapporet is from kipper "atone/cover". "Mercy seat" comes from Tyndale and Luther's Gnadenstuhl. Same in 37:6-9.

kjv: bracelets, and earrings, and rings, and tablets
mine: brooches, earrings, signet rings, and pendants
note: chach is a hook or brooch, and kumaz an ornament of uncertain type, perhaps a pendant or bead necklace. "Tablets" is a guess.

kjv: they were coupled beneath
mine: They were separate beneath
note: to'amim mille-mattah: the Hebrew to'amim ("twins") is read as "doubled/coupled", while many modern readers take the corner frames as paired but distinct below and joined above. The technical sense is uncertain.

kjv: his (the table's) covers to cover withal
mine: its (the table's) jugs for pouring drink offerings
note: haqqesawot 'asher yussakh bahen means "the jugs with which (drink offerings) are poured". The KJV read nasakh "pour" as sakhakh "cover".

kjv: the candlestick
mine: the lampstand
note: menorah is an oil lampstand. There were no candles. Also "knops" (bulbs). The same terms recur through Exodus 25-40.

kjv: of [the women] assembling, which assembled
mine: of the women who served
note: The participle tsove'ot (from tsava, "serve, perform duty") denotes women on duty at the tent entrance (cf. 1 Sam 2:22), not a crowd assembling.

kjv: the gold that was occupied for the work
mine: the gold that was used for the work
note: Hebrew he'asuy means "made/used"; "occupied" meant "employed" in 1611, a sense a modern reader is unlikely to catch.

kjv: cloths of service
mine: finely woven garments
note: Bigdei hasserad: serad is rare and uncertain; it is now usually taken as "woven/plaited (fine) work" applied to garments, not cloths for covering vessels.

kjv: inclosed in ouches of gold
mine: mounted in gold settings
note: Mishbetsot are filigree settings; "ouches" (brooches/settings) is obsolete and opaque to modern readers.

kjv: a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle
mine: carnelian, topaz, and emerald
note: The identification of the breastpiece gems ('odem, pitdah, bareqet, nophek, leshem, etc.) is uncertain in both renderings; "carbuncle" and "ligure" (39:12) reflect Greek/Latin guesses that modern lexicons revise.

kjv: chains at the ends
mine: chains like cords
note: Gavlut is usually derived from "twist/braid" (cf. Exod 28:14), describing cord-like chains; the KJV linked it to gevul "border, end."

kjv: as the hole of an habergeon
mine: like the opening of a coat of mail
note: Takhra is a rare word, probably a leather or mail corselet; "habergeon" is an obsolete term for a sleeveless mail coat.

kjv: badgers' skins
mine: fine leather
note: Tachash is uncertain; badgers are unlikely, and modern scholarship favors a fine leather (possibly dugong/dolphin skin or a dyed leather, cf. Egyptian ths). Context: a fine leather (medium confidence). Tachash is uncertain. It was a valued material (Ezek 16:10, luxury sandals), not a badger's pelt; proposals include an Egyptian loanword for fine or dyed leather and Arabic tuhas 'dolphin/dugong'. 'Fine leather' (NRSV, NET; NIV 'durable leather') commits least to a species. Other possible meanings: (1) sea-cow/dugong or dolphin/porpoise skins — NJPS 'dolphin skins', NASB95 'porpoise skins', NIV 1984 'sea cows'; (2) violet/blue-dyed skins — LXX hyakinthina, Vulgate ianthina; (3) goatskins — ESV; (4) 'badgers' skins' — KJV, from a Talmudic identification of tachash as an animal.

kjv: the meat offering
mine: the grain offering
note: Minchah here is the offering of flour/grain (Lev 2); "meat" in 1611 meant food generally, but modern readers take it as animal flesh. The same KJV term recurs throughout Leviticus.

kjv: he shall offer it of his own voluntary will
mine: so that he may be accepted before Yahweh
note: Lirtsono means "for his acceptance/favour" (ratson, as in 1:4 venirtsah "it will be accepted"), stating the purpose of the offering, not that it is voluntary.

kjv: sprinkle the blood round about upon the altar
mine: splash the blood against all sides of the altar
note: Zaraq means to toss or dash a quantity of liquid, distinct from hizzah "sprinkle" (e.g. 4:6); the KJV uses "sprinkle" for both throughout Leviticus.

kjv: an offering made by fire
mine: a food offering
note: Isheh was traditionally linked to 'esh "fire," but is now often connected with a word for "gift/food offering" (cf. Ugaritic itt); it is also used of non-burnt items like the bread of the Presence (24:7-9). Recurs throughout.

kjv: his (the bird's) crop with his feathers
mine: its (the bird's) crop with its contents
note: Notsah elsewhere means "plumage/feathers," but here it is often taken as the crop's contents or filth (cf. Targum, Rashi); plucking all the feathers would be odd since the bird is burned whole.

kjv: a meat offering
mine: a grain offering
note: Minchah in Leviticus is the cereal offering of flour, oil and frankincense; "meat" meant food in 1611 but now suggests animal flesh, the opposite of what this chapter describes. The KJV uses "meat offering" throughout Leviticus.

kjv: the caul above the liver
mine: the lobe on the liver
note: Yoteret ("appendage") is the caudate lobe of the liver, not the caul (omentum); the KJV followed older guesses. Recurs in 3:10, 3:15, 4:9, 7:4, 8:16, 8:25, 9:10, 9:19.

kjv: the whole rump
mine: the whole fat tail
note: 'Alyah is the broad fat tail of the Near Eastern fat-tailed sheep, removed close to the backbone; "rump" obscures the specific fatty part meant.

kjv: sin through ignorance
mine: sins unintentionally
note: Bishgagah means "inadvertently, by error," covering both ignorance of the law and accidental acts; the KJV's "through ignorance" (also 4:13, 4:22, 4:27, 5:15) narrows it.

kjv: do sin according to the sin of the people
mine: sins, bringing guilt on the people
note: Le'ashmat ha'am means "to the guilt of the people," i.e. the high priest's sin implicates the whole nation; the KJV makes it a sin of the same kind as the people's.

kjv: according to the offerings made by fire
mine: on top of Yahweh's food offerings
note: 'Al ishei YHWH is locative: the fat is burned on top of the offerings already on the altar (cf. 3:5 "on the burnt offering"), not "in the manner of" them.

kjv: hear the voice of swearing
mine: hears a public adjuration to testify
note: Qol 'alah is a public imprecation summoning witnesses to come forward under a curse (cf. Judg 17:2, Prov 29:24); "swearing" now suggests profanity.

kjv: swear, pronouncing with [his] lips
mine: rashly swears with his lips
note: Levatte' means to speak thoughtlessly or rashly (cf. Ps 106:33, Prov 12:18); the law concerns rash oaths, a nuance the KJV's "pronouncing" loses.

kjv: his trespass offering ... for a sin offering
mine: his penalty ... as a sin offering
note: Here 'asham means the penalty or reparation due (the animal is explicitly a sin offering, chatta't); the KJV's "trespass offering" confuses it with the distinct guilt offering of 5:14-19.

kjv: or in fellowship ... or hath deceived his neighbour
mine: or a pledge ... or by extorting from his neighbor
note: Tesumet yad ("placing of the hand") is a pledge or security, not a partnership; 'ashaq means to oppress or extort, not merely deceive. KJV numbers this verse 6:2.

kjv: It [is] the burnt offering, because of the burning upon the altar
mine: The burnt offering shall remain on the hearth on the altar
note: 'Al moqedah means "on the hearth/firewood" (moqedah, place of burning); the KJV read 'al as causal "because of," producing an explanation the text does not give. KJV 6:9.

kjv: with unleavened bread shall it (the grain offering) be eaten
mine: It (the grain offering) shall be eaten unleavened
note: Matsot te'akhel means the remainder itself is eaten as unleavened cakes, not eaten together with unleavened bread. KJV 6:16.

kjv: every one that toucheth them (the offerings) shall be holy
mine: Whatever touches them (the offerings) will become holy
note: Yiqdash can mean "becomes holy" (contagious holiness, so contact is restricted) or "must be holy" (only consecrated persons may touch); the KJV leaves it open but suggests a requirement. KJV 6:18; same in 6:20.

kjv: [and when it is] baken, thou shalt bring it (the grain offering) in
mine: you shall bring it (the grain offering) well soaked
note: Murbekhet (also 7:12) means "well mixed/soaked" with oil, not "baked"; tufinei, rendered "baken pieces," is itself obscure. KJV 6:21.

kjv: it (the sacrifice) shall be an abomination
mine: It (the sacrifice) is a desecrated thing
note: Piggul is a technical term for sacrificial flesh that has become ritually spoiled by being kept too long (cf. 19:7); it is distinct from to'evah, which the KJV also renders "abomination."

kjv: the right shoulder
